## Result: a finite autonomous construction and its matching resource limit

I moved the programme to a more general question exposed by the capture work:

**Can one physical controller coordinate an increasingly large thermal transformation at vanishing energy per controlled unit, while retaining finite kinetics, actual completion quality and complete cycle accounting?**

I obtained a constructive answer within a specified class of autonomous stochastic machines. Shared control can make the fuel cost per unit decrease as \(1/M\). The construction also earns actual completed transformations at finite thermal relaxation. A matching obstruction shows the price: completed-bank throughput decreases as \(1/M\) at fixed kinetics per unit, and as \(1/M^2\) at a fixed total local-update budget.

**This is a completed mathematical construction with ordinary proofs, exact numerical certificates and independent calculations. Its scalable material actuator remains unearned.**

The complete deliverables are:

- [astra_autonomous_control.pdf](https://chatgpt.com/library?file_id=libfile_0db774920640819188b4c7cfeb8572e1&account_id=personal) — the 22-page argument, operating certificates, resource accounting, failed shortcut and primary comparisons.
- [astra_autonomous_control_research.zip](https://chatgpt.com/library?file_id=libfile_ed2cbe886b908191938867b8109a08d1&account_id=personal) — proofs, executable calculations, exact arithmetic, independent audits, source conditions and the unchanged predecessor capture archive.

## 2. The central construction: closing the finite-bath error

The main obstacle was that favorable equilibrium overlap does not establish useful operation with a finite bath.

For each controller phase, let \(\pi_c\) be the known equilibrium distribution of the isolated thermal units. These distributions define a computable reference current \(J_0\). The actual joint stationary distribution generally differs from this reference.

I derived two bounds for the **same full machine**:

\[
|J-J_0|\le C\delta,
\qquad
2\gamma\delta^2\le \sigma_{\mathrm{bath}}\le AJ.
\]

Here \(\delta\) measures the actual tracking error, \(\gamma\) is the finite thermal-refresh rate, and \(C\) is calculated from neighboring equilibrium overlaps and the controller’s rate ceiling.

Combining them gives

\[
|J-J_0|
\le C\sqrt{\frac{AJ}{2\gamma}}.
\]

Solving this inequality yields an explicit positive interval:

\[
R_-(q)J_0\le J\le R_+(q)J_0,
\]

\[
q=\frac{C^2A}{2\gamma J_0},
\qquad
R_-(q)=
\frac{4}{\bigl(\sqrt{q+4}+\sqrt q\bigr)^2},
\qquad
R_+=R_-^{-1}.
\]

The lower bound remains positive at every finite positive bath rate and affinity. No infinitely fast thermal relaxation is assumed.

A separate moment bound controls occupation errors under the actual stationary law. Connecting those errors to first-record low–high–low crossings earns completed-stroke quality as well as controller current.

This is the main scientific addition developed here: **a computable finite-bath current certificate, actual completion quality and complete stationary fuel accounting in one explicit autonomous construction.**

## 1. One complete operating configuration

The machine consists of an \(N\)-state controller coupled to \(M\) binary thermal units. The controller traverses a ring; its position changes the units’ energy bias. Every controller transition retains its reverse transition and depends on the actual thermal load. Each thermal unit relaxes at a finite rate.

All parameters are static in laboratory time. The model supplies one chemical driving affinity, rather than an externally scheduled protocol. Its full stationary entropy production and chemical power satisfy

\[
\sigma=AJ,
\qquad
\dot W=k_BT\,AJ,
\]

where \(J\) is the net rate of controller turns and \(A\) is the total dimensionless chemical affinity per turn. Internal energies and inventories remain stationary.

The canonical finite certificate is:

| Quantity | Simultaneously specified or guaranteed |
|---|---|
| Thermal units | \(M=10{,}000\) |
| Controller states | \(N=200\) |
| Target occupation | \(10\%\rightarrow90\%\rightarrow10\%\) |
| Acceptable completed stroke | At most 2,000 occupied units → at least 8,000 → at most 2,000 |
| Controller kinetics | Each directed jump rate is at most \(\kappa\) |
| Thermal kinetics | Each unit refreshes at rate \(4\kappa\) |
| Total thermal-update capacity | \(40{,}000\kappa\) refresh attempts per unit time |
| Chemical drive | \(A=4\), distributed over 200 steps |
| Guaranteed good-cycle rate | At least \(1.400213392\times10^{-6}\kappa\) |
| Failed record-cycle fraction | At most \(4.570711\times10^{-6}\) |
| Fuel per good completed cycle | At most \(4.000018283\,k_BT\) |

These are conservative analytic guarantees. The numerical inequalities supporting this point use exact rational arithmetic; they do not depend on extrapolating a simulation.

The rate \(\kappa\) is a supplied kinetic parameter. Assigning it an experimental frequency would require a material implementation.

A good cycle is an actual low–high–low excursion of the thermal bank, allowing intermediate reversals. I proved that its long-time counting rate exists and bounded unsuccessful cycles using actual bad-crossing activity. This prevents a turning controller with an effectively stationary load from passing the completion test.
